cooling.h: Almost all the power ends as heat
cooling.p: Servers turn electricity into heat. With cooling and losses, a 1 MW data centre has about 1.4–1.6 MW of heat to get rid of, all the time.
src: industry survey register: pue (LBNL 2023; Uptime 2025 industry survey)

cooling.h: Dry coolers
cooling.p: A closed loop carries the heat to coils outside; fans blow air across them. No water, but they need the most space: 3 units for this size.
texts: fans pull air over the coil
src: operator or maker claim register: component_space (manufacturer claims, equipment only; clearances and switchgear rooms not sourced)

cooling.h: Cooling towers
cooling.p: Warm water falls through the tower and part of it evaporates, which carries the heat away. Smaller and fewer, but it uses water, sends blowdown to the sewer and needs Legionella testing.
src: physics register: evaporation, blowdown (physics: heat ÷ latent heat; cycles of concentration 2–6, FEMP/EPA)

cooling.h: Hybrid (adiabatic) coolers
cooling.p: Dry most of the year. On hot days water is sprayed on the incoming air. In Vancouver that is about 12.4% of the year (1,085 hours above 18 °C).
texts: hot day: water sprayed on the inlet air
Hours with water on, Vancouver (typical year)
src: physics register: evaporation, blowdown (physics: heat ÷ latent heat; cycles of concentration 2–6, FEMP/EPA)

cooling.h: How much room each one takes
cooling.p: Units for 1 MW, with one spare. Area is the units alone; clearances add more.
titles: Dry coolers: 86 m² of units — 3 units
Hybrid coolers: 134 m² of units — 4 units
Cooling towers: 43 m² of units — 3 cells
src: operator or maker claim register: component_space (manufacturer claims, equipment only; clearances and switchgear rooms not sourced)

cooling.h: How much water each one uses
cooling.p: Evaporated on site in a year, at most. Dry coolers use none; towers evaporate up to 1.5 L per kWh of heat.
src: physics register: evaporation, blowdown (physics: heat ÷ latent heat; cycles of concentration 2–6, FEMP/EPA)

heat.p: Air cooling leaves heat at 25–35 °C, too cool for most heating. Liquid cooling to the chip catches 48–75% of it in water.
titles: Caught in liquid: 48–75 % of server heat
Left in the air: 25–52 % of server heat
src: research or government lab register: liquid_capture (LBNL 2014, NREL — direct-to-chip 48–75%; air-cooled: no primary figure)

heat.h: Lifting it with a heat pump
heat.p: A heat pump raises it to about 70 °C for a network. Each unit of electricity gives 3–4.5 units of heat.
src: research or government lab register: cop (DEA 2026 waste-heat heat pumps to 70 °C, 1–3 MW: 3.0–3.6; observed at Meta Odense, 27 → 70 °C: 4.5 in 2020, about 3.9 in 2022–24 — Fjernvarme Fyn annual reports)

heat.p: About 3.2–5.9 GWh a year, the space and water heating of 222–406 homes in Vancouver. Offered is not used: the buildings still have to take it.
src: public record register: homes_heated (NRCan CEUD 2023)

heat.p: 102 buildings that could take heat, by kind. Distance and price decide which are worth a pipe.
src: public record Statistics Canada ODSRF v2 (2026), ODHF (2020), ODEF v2.1 (2022); City of Vancouver non-market housing

energy.p: About 1.4–1.6 MW at the meter on average, 7.4–8.1 GWh a year. The grid sees it as a steady load.

research or government lab register: load_factor (Fan et al. 2007)

energy.p: The same load carries about 19 times the carbon on Alberta's grid as on BC's.
src: public record register: grid_co2 (NIR 2026 Annex 7, consumption intensity 2024)

src: public record register: peak_relief (BC Hydro Demand Response for Business; AESO reserves)

water.p: Only evaporative cooling uses water on site: it evaporates in the tower, and the salts left behind are flushed to the sewer as blowdown.

water.p: At this size, at most. Dry coolers: none.
